utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Registrar, good morning to you. And could you kindly call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is the case number IT-05-88-T, the Prosecutor versus Vujadin Popovic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Madam. Same advisory to all the accused: If at any time during the proceedings you are not receiving interpretation, please draw our attention straight away. Thank you. I see no alterations in the team. Mr. Nicholls is here, and I say it for the record. Yes, are there any preliminaries? Madam Faveau?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAVEAU
utterances.text: [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I can understand what you are saying and the technical problem that you say you have but -- in relation to this witness, but as far as I am concerned, I am not receiving interpretation into English, and that is the second technical problem. And I am on channel 4, so it is not a question of not being --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel please repeat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Faveau, could you kindly repeat your remark or your comment.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. It is actually a technical problem I'd like to put to you. We have received the transcript of the testimony of this witness last week, last Wednesday. We only received the audio recording in B/C/S on Friday. We can't give such recordings to our client until Monday morning, then Monday morning there is the whole procedure of getting audio recording into the Detention Unit, so that they only received it on Tuesday afternoon. They were able to listen to it only yesterday afternoon. My client and others, I believe, have had some problems to open the software in order to listen to the testimony. We're not asking for the trial to be postponed. We're ready to go, but we'd like you assistance for the Prosecutor to provide us with this B/C/S material earlier so that the communication procedure with the Detention Unit be better, smoother, and faster. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Madam Faveau, for pointing that out. Who is going to respond to that? Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I agree, Your Honour, we will try and make sure it isn't provided that late again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Nicholls, and also for your cooperation. And incidentally, those of you who may wish to go last or towards the end of the cross-examination because of this technical problem, please make the necessary arrangements amongst yourselves and you will be accommodated accordingly. Thank you. So the other thing I wanted -- yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Just one small point, Your Honours. I think it was discussed yesterday. We had prepared some map books. The Defence kindly have not objected to those, so those should have been passed out to Your Honours. Those are not yet, I understand, in e-court, but they will be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, they are here. I thank you for them. The only thing I want to mention is that if you intend to make use of these maps with the witness or, for that matter, any other maps or any other photos with witnesses, make sure that if there is an explanation, like there is on this map, "Srebrenica has been Serbian and remains Serbian," et cetera, or "Zepa is also Serbian," or a map with handwritten memos and indications of places and sites, et cetera, that you don't use those maps with the witness. Let the witness mark on maps, but don't give witnesses ready-marked maps which would be tantamount to eliciting information which is already there on the map or on photos. We had the same problems in other cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I understand that, Your Honour. I was thinking about using map 5 in that book with this witness. It does have markings on it and notations. In that case, I will not do that and we'll try to get a different map during the break if I need to use a map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This one I think is harmless, if there is no objection from the Defence. This seems to be a translation of what there is handwritten on the map, so it does not really create a major problem. But if there are other markings --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I think it is map 5, Your Honour, does have some markings on it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah, let me just go through them. But by major problems is when you have, for example, a photo of a destroyed house and then underneath: "House of Mirzad Dudic" and then ask him: Do you recognise this house? for example, all right?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I understand, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Or a photo of some place marked underneath, indicating the location, and then you ask him, the witness: Do you recognise this road in the countryside with the buildings in the background? Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Just on a related issue that might help speed things along. As you know, Mr. Ruez will be testifying soon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And we have in the past had him mark maps prior to him getting into court. It's not the -- sometimes the traditional way, but it does save time and it's not the problem you're talking of, but it's similar. So that is our expectation that he will have -- he will be the one who will have marked the maps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's not the problem I was referring to, definitely. All right. Are there any other preliminaries? I just wanted to confirm to you that later on in the morning we'll be handing down the decision on the e-court filing of cross-examination documents, as per the agreed suggestions. And nothing else, so we can -- yes?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I know everyone's working on it, but the final dates for the confidential programme would help with setting up witnesses. I know that's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah, I think we can go into private session for a couple of minutes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you so much. Yes, I think we can admit the witness. The witness is testifying under the protective measures included in the -- indicated in yesterday's decision - that is with a pseudonym - and we have to decide what number we are going to give him because you've not indicated this in your motion, consequently we did not allocate a pseudonym ourselves. And of course with face distortion. Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I'm sorry we didn't put that in our motion. We -- I believe we're up to PW-110 will be his number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: PW?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: 110, okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'm not sure we need to bring the shutters down when he comes in, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Pardon?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I can't recall if we bring the shutters down because he has a pseudonym.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, we don't need to bring down the curtain, I'm being told, because precautions are taken.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning to you, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And welcome to this Tribunal. Very shortly you will be starting your testimony as a Prosecution witness. As per your request, we have granted you some protective measures. You will not be referred to by your name, but by a nom de plume, a pseudonym. You are going to be Prosecution Witness 110. And anyone who is following the proceedings from outside this courtroom will not be able to see your face because we have a mechanical means of hiding it, as you will see on your own monitor as we go along. Otherwise, the other thing I wanted to tell you is that Madam Usher, who is standing next to you, will be handing to you a solemn declaration, which is tantamount to an oath in various jurisdictions, and that is your undertaking to speak the truth in the course of your testimony. If you at any time require a break, please tell us you're feeling tired, and we will grant you -- we will give you a break.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Please take the solemn declaration and read it out and that will be your undertaking.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. You may sit down. Mr. Nicholls on the Prosecution side will be asking you a series of questions. Please try to keep your replies, your answers, as brief as possible, and when you are being asked for a yes or no answer, stick to that. If you need to go further, let us know and we'll decide whether to give you permission or not. Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: The first order of business, if I could have the assistance of an usher, is to show the witness the pseudonym sheet.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Sir, please read that to yourself silently, and I'll ask you: Can you confirm that your name is written on that sheet of paper which you've been handed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Would you kindly show it to the members of the Defence teams, and then it will be handed to the registrar, who will enter it into the records as a sealed document. Registrar, could you please indicate to us which number you are going to give it, which exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I understand in the future, Your Honour, these will also be in the e-court system.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah, do you want to see it, Mr. Nicholls?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. So this will become Exhibit Number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit Number P2101 [Realtime transcript read in error "P2102"].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: P210 -- that's correct, then, because on the transcript it's P2102 and I heard you say P2101.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour; P2101.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. That's corrected. Mr. Nicholls, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. I request we go into private session for some preliminary background.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, let's go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. We are in open session now, Witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Sir, how long did you stay in Konjevic Polje?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110
utterances.text: I was six days in Konjevic Polje, and during those six days I believe that Mr. Morillon came, the commander of UNPROFOR forces, and he went up there to a mosque in Hrncici. I don't know exactly because I'm not familiar with the area. I believe it was the Hrncici mosque. This is where he hoisted up the UN flags. And then the Serbs who were in Tumace opened fire on the population right before Morillon's face. I'm not 100 per cent sure, but I believe that one UNPROFOR soldier was seriously hurt. There were a lot of people killed, a lot of people injured. Morillon was there and he was watching that with his own two eyes. If he was a good man, he would be sitting here today and he would testify to the event that happened right before his eyes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. That was a bit of a long answer to the question, but thank you. Now, where did you go from Konjevic Polje?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110
utterances.text: After that, we moved to Pervane. That's where we stayed for three days. And then a decision was issued. Everybody started withdrawing towards Srebrenica. I and my two brothers arrived in Srebrenica on the 14th of March.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: While in Srebrenica, did you do any kind of work, you personally?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110
utterances.text: Yes, I worked as a farm worker. We had a horse, a cow. We had the cow for milk and the horse to carry stuff for us, and that was that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: You said you went with two of your brothers. Were either of your brothers in the --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Please wait -- thank you, but please wait for me to finish the question. Was either of your brothers in the army, the Bosnian army, in the enclave?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110
utterances.text: The one who had not arrived, he was a cook -- actually, a baker in a private store in the village, throughout all that time. In my own village, he was also a cook, he was never a soldier.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay, just to be clear, are you saying he was a cook for the army in the enclave?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110
utterances.text: Yes, yes. He was a member of the -- some sort of reserves. I'm not a hundred per cent sure. The enclave was under the patronage of the United Nations, the arms had been distributed, and he was acting as a cook. He was something as a cook there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It is not clear. What time are we talking about here? Is it still March, 1993, or later? Because he refers to Srebrenica being an enclave under the patronage of the United Nations. If it's after 16th April, we're talking of the period of demilitarisation, and he speaks of arms being distributed instead of arms being collected. Perhaps he could clarify all this.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no. The arms had been collected by UNPROFOR. There was just an observation point at a most critical point. They didn't have arms. Whoever was seen with arms by UNPROFOR, the arms would be seized from them by UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That makes it clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: From the time you arrived until July, 1995, was your brother a cook for the army, or reserve as you called them, in the -- in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110
utterances.text: He was only observing. They could not hold arms because of the UNPROFOR. They only had an observation point in an area that I am not familiar with. I never went there, and that's the only thing they were doing, they were just observing, without any arms.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Listen to my question, please. I'm asking if your brother worked as a cook for these reserves until July, 1995.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes. He was a cook. He was always a cook, before that and during that time. He was never a soldier. He was always a cook, just a cook.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now I want to talk a little bit about how you came to leave Srebrenica. When did you leave Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110
utterances.text: When the Serbs started coming in in order to occupy Srebrenica. We left on the 11th of July in the morning. Some went towards Potocari, some of us went through the woods. On the 11th of September, the entire population - I apologise, it was in July - on the 11th of July, the whole population left Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Very briefly - very briefly - describe to me what the week before July 11th was like for the inhabitants of Srebrenica. What was going on?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110
utterances.text: Well, the area was rife with panic, and the people moved from the upper part of Srebrenica. They all came to Vidikovac and lower down. From Sunday till Tuesday, nobody was there, save for some bedridden people, people who could not leave their houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, were there any announcements made that you heard, about leaving on the 11th of July?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110
utterances.text: No, no, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: You said that some people went to Potocari and some people went into the woods --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110
utterances.text: Yes. Women, children, and the elderly went to Potocari. I don't know if any younger people went there as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Where did you go?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110
utterances.text: I went in the direction of the village of Susnjari. There we formed a column and proceeded towards the free territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I just thought perhaps a redaction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, because I was marking -- making a mark.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Not a huge issue, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, okay. Yeah. That's -- there isn't much of it, but I think we need to redact line -- from line 16 to 18; I would redact the three of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, sir, what about your other brother? Where did he go?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110
utterances.text: My other brother was an invalid. He went to Potocari. And luckily for him, although they kept people behind, he was allowed to go and he went from there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: When you say "they kept people behind," some people, who's "they"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110
utterances.text: Serb soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Are you okay, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110
utterances.text: Yes, but my headphones keep moving on my head. Otherwise, I'm okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Usher, please, if you could kindly make the necessary adjustments for him. Mr. Nicholls, and any of the Defence teams that are nearer to the witness than we are, usually we can more or less have a very close visual view of his face on the monitor, but when it's -- visual -- face distortion, we can't. And you're much nearer to him than we are. If you notice any sign of tiredness or need for a break, please draw our attention straight away.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Because we can't see as much as we would see under normal circumstances, in other words.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: There used to be an option to see the undistorted video in the courtroom. I don't know if that is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, we don't have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Perhaps that's correct, Your Honour. Private session just for one moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. So let's redact from line 5, please -- from line 6 to here, and let's go into private session for a while.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are in public session again. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. Now I want to talk to you about something you spoke about earlier, the formation of the column in Susnjari, and the night of the 11th to 12th of July in Susnjari. Now, where did you sleep that night?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110
utterances.text: In Susnjari.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: But where in Susnjari? What type of place did you sleep in?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110
utterances.text: In a meadow, where everybody was, all the men who had arrived there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And how many men was that, approximately?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110
utterances.text: According to an estimate, there must have been at least 15.000 men.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Is that your estimate or an estimate you heard?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110
utterances.text: Well, we talked amongst each other. We looked at each other. We thought that there may have well been over 15.000 people, even 20.000, maybe.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Was it all men or were there any other women or children in this column?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110
utterances.text: At that time, there were neither women nor children there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: What time did you leave Susnjari? I mean the --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110
utterances.text: I left in the afternoon, on the 12th of July. I was with the last group of people who left Susnjari.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And where was your other brother at this time? Don't say his name.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110
utterances.text: He was there. He was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: With you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Can you just describe for us a little bit, so we get a picture, the terrain that you and all these men were walking through in the direction towards Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110
utterances.text: We were walking in a column -- actually, in several columns. Not -- sometimes we were walking single file because of the way the terrain looked.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And were any men in this column armed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110
utterances.text: Yes. There were very few armed men, and those men walked with the front of the columns. They left with the first columns that left.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Were you able to form an estimate of how many men were armed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110
utterances.text: Maybe 400 or 500. It was very difficult to tell with so many people being there. It was difficult to tell how many people were armed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I understand, sir. I didn't -- I wouldn't expect you to know an exact number. What kind of weapons were they armed with?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110
utterances.text: Infantry.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Infantry what? If you could explain what --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110
utterances.text: Rifles. They mostly had rifles.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Were you armed? Did you have a rifle?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: What about your brother?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: What did you bring with you as you -- as you set out on this trek?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110
utterances.text: A rucksack, and I had three tins of meat that I had received from humanitarian aid. I had a spare jacket across my shoulder and a sack of sugar. That's all I had.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And now if you could just look -- sorry. You had a jacket -- or a spare jacket. What kind of clothes were these? Were they military? Civilian? Could you describe your clothing.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110
utterances.text: No, I wore civilian clothes. I wore a leather jacket, a pair of trousers, some shoes. I can't remember exactly. What I had on my shoulder was a rucksack; that's all I had.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And then you said you left in the afternoon of the 12th. Describe a little bit that day in your own words where you went and what you did.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110
utterances.text: I'm telling you, on that same day we left Susnjari and we walked until the sun set, when we could no longer see. I did not sleep at all that night. I did not sleep the previous day, and I had not slept the previous night, and then I lie down and slept that night. When the day broke, my brother was no longer there. Some people were on their way back. Some were moving forward. I returned a little, and then some people started moving forward. I went with them. I found my brother there. We sat down. We discussed as to what should be done. In the meantime, the Serb soldier took a megaphones and --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Let me stop you. Thank you. We'll get to those other parts of what happened next. Do you know approximately where you spent the night of 12th/13th July? You said you hadn't had much sleep, you laid down. Where did you spend the next night?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110
utterances.text: In the forest called Buljim.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: So now we come to the 13th July. You started describing how you woke up that morning. Let's start with where was your brother that morning when you woke up? You began to talk about that.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110
utterances.text: I'm telling you, a group of people returned, and I returned with them. And then the same group of people moved forward. I went with them and he was a bit further down, close to the area where we exited from the woods, this Samici, Lolici, I haven't a clue what the name is.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: The transcript says "Samici." I think you said "Sandici."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110
utterances.text: Not Samici. Sandici is the name.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you for pointing that out, Mr. Nicholls. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: If I can just clarify one moment, Witness, your last answer. You woke up, your brother wasn't there, you moved with some other people [Realtime transcript read in error "brother"], and then you were reunited with your brother. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, you said the area where you exited the woods was something like Sandici or Lolici, you're not sure what the name is. Tell me about how you came to be --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110
utterances.text: No, no. No. It was also in Buljim, but when we went down, when we surrendered, it was in Sandici. It was also Buljim, the place where I found my brother.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I understand Buljim to be the name of the forest, if I understand him well. Yes, Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would just like to get some clarification. I'm looking at the question that was put by my colleague at page 27, line 4. Of course it's kind of a leading question, but that's not the point of my objection. I'd just like to get clarification, because I don't quite get the question. It says: "Could you clarify. You woke up, your brother wasn't there, you moved with some other brother, and then you were reunited with your brother." And then the answer is yes, but I fail to understand this part.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, no, you're a hundred per cent right. It's the transcript which is wrong. He never said I moved with another brother, he moved with some others and then he was reunited with the brother. So it's the transcript that needs to be corrected.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I thank my colleague for pointing out --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank Mr. Bourgon as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Please describe how you came to leave the woods and how you ended up in Sandici.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110
utterances.text: As I told you, the dawn broke, the Serb soldiers took up megaphones, and started calling out to us to surrender. There were people in camouflage uniforms amongst us who said: Yes, we will surrender, but bring UNPROFOR and the Red Cross over. However, they made no promises; rather, they issued an ultimatum to the effect that we should surrender by 10.00 or else. Since we did not surrender until 10.00, we were issued with another ultimatum to surrender by 3.00 in the afternoon. It was at that point that we decided to surrender ourselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. Let me ask you a quick follow-up question. You said you were up in woods and the Serb soldiers took up megaphones and started calling out to you to surrender. Where were they calling from, these Serb soldiers? Where were they?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110
utterances.text: They were a bit further away from us, but in the same general area, in the same field. This was a rather large mountain, woodland, and it would take you a couple of hours to cross it through, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And you say you decided to surrender. What about your brother; what did he decide to do?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110
utterances.text: He decided the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And then what did you do? What happened?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110
utterances.text: The column set out to surrender. As we came down there, the Serb soldiers approached us and asked us for any money that we might have in all foreign currencies. They threatened us that if we should not surrender all our money, we would suffer the same fate as those before us. Of course we didn't ask who those before us were or what happened to them. As we went along, there were women and children passing by in a bus. I knew some of the women on the bus, and they were looking at us just as I'm looking at you now. They went away whilst we remained there as prisoners.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. I was going to talk about that a little bit later, but let's talk about it now. How many buses did you see with, as you say, women and children passing by?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110
utterances.text: Several vehicles went by. There was my aunt there, another lady from Drinjaca near Zvornik. There was one -- third lady that I didn't know, but she told my brother that we had been captured.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Which direction were these buses going in on this road?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110
utterances.text: They went toward Vlasenica and the free territory there. That was where the women and children were transported to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Nicholls, I wonder if you could clarify with the witness whether there were some armed people when they surrendered to the Serb forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I was -- I will do that now.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: If you heard Your Honour's comments, sir, were there any armed men in the column at this point you surrendered?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110
utterances.text: No, no. There was one person among us who had military boots on, and he was immediately criticised for it by Serb soldiers, but none of us had any camouflage uniforms. This person wearing military boots had them by necessity, of course, because probably he didn't have any other footwear. It was summertime and it was very hot. It must have been very uncomfortable for him.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Well, that aside, then, just to be clear, did anybody have any rifles at the time of this surrender? I think you answered it, but I want it to be very clear.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, did you know at the time that where 400, 500 who had been armed went?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They went off in the first column. We didn't know where they were. This particular column had been cut off from us, which of course we weren't aware of at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And I'll ask one question to try to continue to clarify that. I think you answered this before, Witness, but where in the overall column were you and your brother?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110
utterances.text: I myself was perhaps somewhere halfway through the column.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And is that the whole column or your segment of the column? Because you said it broke up.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110
utterances.text: No, no. Do you mean when we were surrendering? When we were surrendering, I was in the last column to leave Susnjari.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. All right. Now, you talked a moment ago about soldiers demanding money and foreign currency. What happened next after that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110
utterances.text: We raised our arms. They told us to move, running, and people were already seated in the meadow there. We were simply filling out the ranks. There was one Serb soldier who had this red ribbon. He seemed to be the main person there. He said: We were already negotiating for your exchange with other -- with the UNPROFOR. And there was a young man there who told me some 10 or 15 minutes later, when we saw women and children on the buses passing there, he --

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I apologise. I hate to interrupt the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: But it seems we have some problems. I believe that the witness is speaking too fast and it does cause some problems to the interpreters, because we understand his language and we know what he's talking. Well, let me just make one brief example. The witness just said that the person with the -- the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The red ribbon.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: -- that the governments are negotiating. Instead of this, we read here that "we are negotiating with UNPROFOR," and it basically does --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, no, it does make a difference, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: -- make a difference.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you for your observation and for your help, Mr. Lazarevic. Mr. Nicholls -- first of all, I do wish to have a confirmation from the interpreter's booth.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, this may have been the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, exactly. So I understand, Witness, that you need to speak a little bit more slowly. Let me --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's the way I speak, and I do consider it to be slow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But it's not slow enough. Let me explain to you what the problem is. Here, when I speak in English, as I am doing now, what I am saying has to be translated by people behind the windows that you see on the sides into your language - otherwise you would not understand what I am saying - and it has to be translated also into the French language for those who are following in French. Similarly, when you are speaking in Serbo-Croat, the interpreters have to translate to us in English and they have to catch up with the speed of your delivery of -- so the slower you speak, the better it is for them to be able to catch and translate every single word that you say. No one is criticising the way you speak or that this is -- we are trying to make it difficult for you, but we're just asking you to slow down a little bit more so that you make the interpreters' task a little bit easier. All right? And I am sure you will cooperate in this. Okay. I thank you. Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And once more, thank you, Mr. Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes, sir, please, I'll try to speak a little bit slower. Maybe we both can. We want the record to be as accurate as it can be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah, and I think it's the case of going through this part again, since, as Mr. Lazarevic pointed out, it's not correct or it -- let me go through it. You were asked this question, sir. Mr. Nicholls asked: "Okay. All right. Now, you talked a moment ago about soldiers demanding money and foreign currency. What happened next after that?" And then you started answering. You said: "We raised our arms. They told us to move, running, and the people were already seated in the meadow there." Do you confirm this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Then in the transcript we have the following: "We were simply filling out the ranks." Do you confirm that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And then I have: "There was one Serb soldier who had this red ribbon," a bandanna. Do you confirm that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was black.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So that's the first item that needs to be corrected. And then also in relation to this Serb soldier you are reported to having said: "He seemed to be the main person there." Correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: "And he said: We were already negotiating for your exchange with other -- with the UNPROFOR." Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no. No, none of us told us [as interpeted] there were negotiations with the UNPROFOR, but rather that the negotiations were in course between the Serb and Bosnian governments -- Bosniak government.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. And then we have: "And there was a young man there who told me some 10 minutes or 15 minutes later, when we saw women and children on the buses passing there --" and you were stopped in -- at that point.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not a young man. There was a woman with a child aged 10. This man with the black bandanna told the lady to go down there where the bus was parked. We weren't able to see the bus because of the lay of the terrain. The lady -- the woman thanked the soldier for it. Two young girls also stood up. One that was more beautiful of the two --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Stop right there. We'll get to that. We're getting a bit ahead.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. And I thank Mr. Lazarevic again. And if there are substantive mistakes in the transcript, please draw our attention straight away. If they are minor mistakes that can be rectified later, let's not waste time on them. We will attend to them later on. But any substantive mistakes in the transcript from what the witness is testifying are important to be noted down immediately. Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Could I ask Your Honours to ask the booth if the problem is the speed the witness is talking or if there is any other problem, because "UNPROFOR" and "government" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, I don't need to put the question now. They have heard you. It seems that the problem, at least as far as I can say, because I am not following the proceedings in French, is the translation in the English -- translation from B/C/S to English. If you could indicate to me what the problem is -- first of all, where is the -- that's okay. I think it's there, if I can see well. What is the problem?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: It was the speed, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The speed. Okay. So as you can see, Witness, it's the speed that has complicated matters. If you can slow down again, as I asked you to do earlier on, it would be very important.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will try to slow down a bit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. And if at any time, Madam Interpreters, he is going too fast, please draw my attention straight away. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I spoke we go to 10.30?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, sir, approximately how many men came out of the woods and surrendered in this incident you've been discussing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110
utterances.text: According to an estimate, there must have been over a thousand of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: When you reached the meadow where you say you were -- sat down, was the meadow empty, or were there already prisoners there when you arrived?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110
utterances.text: There were prisoners there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: How many would you estimate were already there when you arrived?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110
utterances.text: Perhaps about 500 of them, but others kept coming in.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, were you able to sit anywhere you wanted in this meadow or were you told where to sit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110
utterances.text: No. Wherever there was an empty spot. We were just filling out the ranks.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. And were there any soldiers at this field? Serb soldiers, I mean.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110
utterances.text: Yes. The ranks were about 20 or more metres long, and every single row was guarded by two soldiers at each end of the row.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Row of prisoners, you mean?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110
utterances.text: Yes, yes, prisoners.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, you've explained well that you were told that negotiations were taking place between the governments for an exchange. Did that -- and then you started to tell us about how that soldier sent one woman and her child to a bus to get on. Can you finish telling me about any people who left the meadow.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110
utterances.text: When the soldier ordered the lady and the child to leave, he -- she stood and thanked him. There were two young girls there, too. When they stood up, the Serb soldiers who were there told the more beautiful of the two that she should -- they told this particular soldier that she should stay behind. However, the Serb soldier did not listen to them. He told the girls and the lady to leave. There were about a dozen young boys who also stood up, but then the soldier told them: No, no, you should sit down because you're capable of carrying a machine-gun.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. I think this is a point that might need clarification. How many boys stood up -- you started talking about some boys who stood up to leave. How many of them were there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110
utterances.text: About a dozen. I don't know precisely. I didn't count them, but there were about a dozen of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Were any of them allowed to leave of these boys?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110
utterances.text: Pardon?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Were any of these dozen boys allowed to leave and get on buses?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110
utterances.text: Oh, yes. They left, the dozen of them, perhaps a bit more or a bit less than ten. I didn't count them all. I didn't know what was to come. Had I known what was ahead of us, I would have tried my best to memorise things better.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: That's all right. Nobody -- at least, I don't expect you to remember everything from what happened 11 years ago. How many boys were told to sit down because they could carry a machine-gun?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110
utterances.text: I think there was just one.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: About how old were the boys who were allowed to leave and were allowed to get on the buses?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110
utterances.text: I think that none of them had -- were 15 yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, on this meadow, how many -- how long did you spend there before you were -- before you went someplace else?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110
utterances.text: We stayed there for a couple of hours at least.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: During that time, were you provided with any food?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Were you - and by "you" I mean the prisoners collectively - provided with any water?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110
utterances.text: Everyone was given water, but I don't know if they had received enough because we just couldn't get enough water with the thirst that there was.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, were you able to see whether there were any wounded prisoners or any prisoners who looked as though they needed medical treatment?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110
utterances.text: Yes. There were wounded there. People were asking for bandages from the soldiers, but the soldiers told them: No. Well, if you are -- can manage to find some bandages on your own, well, fine. But they wouldn't provide us with anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: While you were on that meadow, was there any kind of physical abuse of the prisoners by the soldiers?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: It might be better to break now, Your Honour, if that's okay, because I think the next little chunk might not finish in five minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Certainly, Mr. Nicholls. We'll have a 30-minute break because there were some redactions, and because of that we need 30 minutes. Yes, Mr. Meek.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: I apologise, Your Honour. I was just trying to get Steve's attention.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Yes. Thank you. Do we need -- because since there are members of the public in the gallery, I suppose we need to put the curtains down before the witness is -- leaves the courtroom. Alternatively, the guards can ask the members of the public to leave the gallery now, and it will spare us having to put down the curtains. Wait, wait, wait, Usher. And the cameras are not to focus on the witness as he exits the courtroom. Thank you. There will be a break of 30 minutes from now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: We left off before the break, sir, we were still talking about the time you were held prisoner in the meadow at Sandici. While you were there, did any senior officers arrive at the meadow?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Can you describe that, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110
utterances.text: As we were sitting on the meadow, this was close to the dusk, General Mladic arrived. I didn't know him at the time, but certain persons --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness explain who.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- told us that Mladic had arrived. He told us, "Good evening, Neighbours." He also promised and said our governments were negotiating and tomorrow you should all be exchanged, all for all. He told us that we were to go to certain hangars. The soldier wearing a black bandanna told us that we would receive some supper, but Mladic said, No, you're not going to get any supper, you're just going to get some water. Then he went away. Let me just say this once again: When he told us that we would be exchanged the following day, all for all, we applauded him and said, Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. Again I'll remind you to please, if you can - I know it's difficult - to speak a little bit slower than you normally would. Who was it who told you this person you hadn't seen before was General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110
utterances.text: Persons who were captured, who I -- I hadn't seen him before.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Did you ever see a picture of General Mladic after these events?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110
utterances.text: I did. Later on, when he came to Potocari I saw it on TV when I went to the free territory. And I'm a hundred per cent sure that that was Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: We'd also finished, and you had explained to Their Honours that there was no physical abuse of the prisoners in the meadow. Was there any kind of humiliating treatment that you observed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110
utterances.text: No. Only one person who was sitting on the transporter told us: Let me not shoot you all and go straight to The Hague, because at that time that was already something that existed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. Now, I'd like to have you please explain to us how you came to leave the meadow, you personally, and what you could see how the other prisoners left as well.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110
utterances.text: When they wanted to transport us from there, the lorries and the buses that transported the women and the children and returned empty, a command was issued, the first line run to the vehicles and load them, the second line, and then all the way up to my line. And then I stood up. I ran down the hill. They told us to get on the lorry. I got into the trailer behind the lorry - it had high sides - and I saw a Serbian soldier with a black cap, and he told us that he would get on with the driver. And as a vehicle was full, it would leave. And as soon as it was dark, we were driving up the hill and we saw vehicles moving by us. We didn't know who they were, what vehicles those were. And when we arrived in Bratunac, one driver who was there told us: Those are Vihor's garages on the left-hand side. We could see the buildings on the right-hand side. We couldn't see anything. We did not dare lift our heads or put our hand on the sides of the trailer. Then the Serb soldiers surrounded the vehicles, and they started asking whether there were -- there was anybody from the villages around Srebrenica, for example, Husmanici, Potocari, Slatina, Bljeceva. Glogova was also mentioned. In the meantime, if somebody appeared, they would ask his father's name --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. Again, I know it's difficult. Please try to speak a little more slowly. We want everything to be captured by the interpreters and captured by our transcript. So please continue a little bit more slowly.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110
utterances.text: And then, as a person appeared, they would take him away. And the driver who was with us in the same trailer, he told us: These are Vihor's garages. I don't know to this very day where those garages are. And he was a driver by profession. I don't know who he was affiliated with, but I know he was a driver. And as the person was taken up there, we would hear a blunt hit and the person would start crying out and wailing.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Let me ask you a couple questions now.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Your Honour, could we go into private session for one moment?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Let's go into private session for a while, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are in open session. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Let me ask you a few follow-up questions, sir, about your journey to these Vihor garages. Which direction were the trucks, one of which you were on, going on the road? Which direction were they going as they took you away? Towards which town?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110
utterances.text: Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: You said that a driver told you once the vehicles -- excuse me, the lorry had parked, that it was Vihor's garages where you were.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110
utterances.text: Yes. The one who was captured together with us, he told us that. I know his name, if you want me to tell you his name, and I know where he is from. I had not met him before. I only met him in Srebrenica. But I can tell you his name.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: That's what I wanted to clarify. The driver was a fellow prisoner who worked as a driver; it wasn't the driver of the truck who brought you to Vihor's garages?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110
utterances.text: That's correct, yes. He was not the driver of that vehicle.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: You said that the vehicle had high sides, the truck you were in. Did it have a roof?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110
utterances.text: Yes, high sides but no roof. It was open -- an open lorry. There were just some boards on the bottom, and that's all it had. Those boards were there so as to have the women and the children not sitting on the very bottom of that trailer. And that's all the trailer and the lorry had.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. Approximately how many men were in your trailer?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110
utterances.text: There were at least 30 to 40 people there. We could not stretch our legs. We had to sit very tight. The lorry was rather long, that trailer was rather long.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Once you were parked at the Vihor's garages, could you -- were you able to see out of the truck or were the sides too high?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110
utterances.text: Nobody was allowed to lift their heads, and unless you lifted your head you couldn't see a thing. That's how high the sides were. As we were sitting down in the lorry, we could not see anything without lifting our heads, which we didn't dare do.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Did anybody try to look out?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110
utterances.text: I only heard somebody putting their hand on the side of the lorry and was immediately hit with a rifle. Nobody else dared repeat that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: From what you could hear, were you able to estimate how many other trucks were parked alongside the lorry or trailer that you were in?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110
utterances.text: There was a column of vehicles parked there. I don't know how many vehicles were there. Only on the following day could I see how long the column is, as we were climbing up the hill. I don't know whether all the vehicles were there, whether we were all there, or whether some other -- some vehicles went in some other directions. I didn't know at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. You were talking about how you could hear people being called out according to which village they came from, their names, and then you would hear sounds of, you said thuds, I think, and screams and shouts. Can you describe just briefly to us how that worked. Who was coming and asking -- calling out names of villages and calling out names of people?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110
utterances.text: We couldn't hear people introducing themselves. They went from one vehicle to another. They came to our vehicle and asked whether there was somebody from Srebrenica. Nobody was taken out of my lorry until the next morning, and if somebody answered, they would take them away. They would hit them with the rifle butts, they would threaten them. And as they took them to the garage, which was some 50 metres away from our vehicle, and when we heard those thuds, then these men started screaming and then they would start yelling: Stop that, stop that. And then we would hear a burst of fire, and this lasted the whole night. In the course of the night, one Serb soldier jumped on the trailer and did not ask for people from various villages. He was very specific and said whether there was anybody from Srebrenica. One person stood up. I know his name because I knew him. Our fields were next to each other, and he said: I was from Srebrenica. And the person asked him: Which village are you from? And he said from Ljeskovik. And then he said: Sit down. He did not want to take that person away. That person was older than me at the time. He may have been the same age as I am now.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. While you were kept there on these trucks that night, were you given any food?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110
utterances.text: No, never, never. We were never offered any food.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Were you given any water?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And was there any offer of medical treatment to anybody that you saw who might have needed help?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, you said the next morning someone was taken off your truck. Did you spend the whole night on the truck?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110
utterances.text: The whole night. In the morning, the soldiers started shouting: Don't let the civilians get away. Because I suppose they were afraid that the civilians might have talked about the massacre. And they said: Don't let the civilians anywhere near. And when it dawned, one Serb soldier jumped on the trailer and said to one person which was in the left corner, and he said: Where are you from? And he said: Omer, and I don't know whether that was his name or his father's name. And then the soldier said: Come off the truck. He took him away. The person got off the truck. And then from the right-hand side they took another young man. They had recognised him. I don't know who that Serbian soldier was. I didn't know him, and he took that young man away from the trailer. And then they started shouting: Take them to Fikret and Halija. The Serbs speak in a different way. They had H's where it is necessary. Instead of Alija they said Halija and instead of Halid they said Alid, and they said, okay, take them to Fikret and Halija and have them exchanged.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Well, since I was invited by the Trial Chamber to do some comment, to be honest, even I didn't quite understand what the witness was talking about even though I understand the language. Frankly I understood that some civilians -- I didn't understand whether he was saying that some civilians were trying to approach these detainees, or what was this all about? If we can go through this again. I really don't know what that was all about.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I can ask that question again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, please do, Mr. Nicholls. I thank you, Mr. Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Again, sir, please, as much as you can, try to speak a little bit more slowly. You spoke about hearing in the morning: Don't let the civilians -- hearing the soldiers shouting: Don't let the civilians get away. And that you were --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110
utterances.text: No, no. The civilians were the local Serbs residing in Bratunac. Those were not civilians from Srebrenica. Those were the local Serb civilians, the locals of Bratunac. There was a building there. As we arrived that evening, one young man peaked through the window and an elderly lady pulled a curtain on the window so as to prevent the child looking through the window. Those were the Serbs -- Serb residents of Bratunac. There were no Bosniak residents of Bratunac at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: So what you heard the soldiers saying was that they needed to keep the Bratunac Serb civilians away from the trucks and the prisoners.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110
utterances.text: They didn't say "Serbs," they only said: Don't let the civilians come up here to that street. They didn't allow their own civilians to go there. They were not referring to the Bosniak civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Could we go into private session for just one moment?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's go into private session for a while, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. We are back in open session, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'd like you to tell the Court now how you came to leave --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, because I don't think we have covered the totality of Mr. Lazarevic's observation. So we've cleared one thing; namely, that in the morning some of the soldiers were asking or shouting that the civilians should not be allowed to come near the trucks. We've cleared that. We've also cleared this last point that we had in private session. But then earlier on when he was testifying, he said: "And when it dawned --" at dawn, in other words -- "one Serb soldier jumped on the trailer and said to one person who was in the left corner, and he said: Where are you from? And he said: Omer." So this he needs to clarify. Do you confirm this, first of all, Witness? Do you confirm that at dawn or just after dawn one Serb soldier jumped on the trailer and asked one of you who was on the left corner: Where are you from? Do you confirm this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it was not the soldier who jumped on the trailer. He jumped on the back of the lorry, and he recognised that prisoner. And I don't know whether his name was Omer or his father's name was Omer, but this soldier recognised that person. It was already daylight, and then he ordered that person to get off. And then they -- this person also probably recognised the other man, the young man on the right-hand side. He didn't ask the question that they had been putting the previous evening, and that was what villages we were from. They recognised two people on the trailer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I believe that the main misunderstanding was about the question that the soldier posed to these men. We have here in transcript the question allegedly posed was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: "Where are you from?"

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: -- "Where are you from?" But actually what I heard is the question was: "What is your father's name?" And the witness did not understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. This is why it is important that you slow down as much as you can, Witness. I know it's difficult sometimes. It's difficult for me, too, but let's try a little bit better. Make a next try of it. So the question by this Serb soldier was not -- to this young man was not: "Where are you from?" But: "What's your father's name?" Do you agree to that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. He asked him about either his own name or his father's name. That's why I'm not clear whether Omer was his name or his father's name. The questions differed in the evening from those that were put in the morning. In any case, I know that this soldier recognised this man.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So this -- thank you. This person was then taken off the truck. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And he was taken away. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And then you had continued, saying that -- "and then from the right-hand side they took another young man. They had recognised him. I don't know who that Serbian soldier was. I didn't know him, and he took that young man -- and they took that young man away from the trailer." Do you agree to this? Do you confirm this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. He took him away just like the previous one. I don't know where he took them, I haven't a clue, because we did not dare lift our heads over the trailer side to observe what was going on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And then we have another part in the transcript which is very confusing and you need to clear it up for us, please. And then you continued stating: "And then they started shouting: Take them to Fikret and Halija." Then we have got something missing. So what did they say? Take them to ...?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Take them to Halija and Fikret and have them exchanged.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Did Fikret and Alija mean anything to you at the time when --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] How could it mean anything? We were prisoners. It didn't mean anything to us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And then you are reported as saying here in the transcript: "The Serbs speak in a different way." Did you say those words? And if you did, what did you mean --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's what I said. I'm just quoting what they said. An educated person uses correct grammar. If a word starts with an A, then they will start their words with an A. If they are not educated, then they would add an H before that A, and the other way around. I lived all my life with the Serbs, and I know that the Serb villagers talk like that. If a person is educated, an educated Serb would not say Halija if he is supposed to say Alija.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I think the rest of the transcript does not need any further clarification. It's self-explanatory. Let's proceed now. Yes, Mr. Nicholls, he is all yours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, remembering, please, try to speak slowly. Tell me about how you left Vihor's garages, where the truck -- trucks went.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110
utterances.text: When we set off in the morning, the lorries started moving towards an exit from Bratunac. The column stopped at the moment, and at one point we heard them shouting: We're waiting for the UNPROFOR. And this is where we were sitting. It was very hot. The sides were made of metal. The driver was very correct, he often brought us water, and he was joined by a 15- or 16-year-old man from Bratunac, and he also brought us water. And that young lad asked if there was an Ismet there, and I believe his family name was Ramic. He was a shoemaker from Bratunac. Some people who were imprisoned with us asked him: Why are you asking after Ismet? And he said: He is my neighbour. And while we were standing there, a lorry that was in Srebrenica that was transporting humanitarian aid - it was an old truck - a group of elderly Serbs appeared. Their average age was over 60. Some of them wore uniforms. They wore the uniforms of the former JNA, and the others did not wear uniforms. They were all standing there, and since the sides of the lorry were very tall, as they started passing by the lorry, they started shouting: These are our people. What did they mean by that, I don't know. And then that lorry went away. We probably waited there for two or three hours. I don't know. At the time I didn't have a watch. And then the column started moving on towards Konjevic Polje. As we drove by the -- by Avdaga's field and we started climbing up the hill, then I could see how long the column of vehicles was. After that we were not stopped anywhere. We passed Konjevic Polje and Drinjaca, and when we arrived at Josanica, where there is the stone quarry, some people saw, either before the tunnel or after the tunnel --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Slow down. Because even I who don't understand your language can sense the speed that you are going at. So please slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Let me ask you a question, sir. You said you were stopped for two to three hours, and you said in the beginning of your answer that this was at an exit near Bratunac. I want to be clear: Is that where you waited --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110
utterances.text: Yes, yes, from Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: So you waited for two to three hours at the exit from Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110
utterances.text: Yes. That's where we were stopped and that's where we waited all that time. They said that they were waiting for UNPROFOR; that's what we heard.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you talked about how at one point during this journey you could see, because you were going up a hill, how long the convoy of lorries or trucks was. How many -- if you remember, about how many trucks were there in this convoy?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110
utterances.text: There was also a column of buses -- or rather, there were buses in the column, and there must have been at least 20 vehicles in the column, as it was very long, even 30.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, you were just starting to tell us about something that happened when you got to -- I think you said to a tunnel by Zvornik. Could you explain where you were and what happened.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110
utterances.text: As we reached Josevac on the road to Josanica, there's a large quarry there and we set out for Divic. As we came out of the tunnel someone saw that there was an APC near the Vidikovac Hotel, which was about 800 metres away from where we were. We continued our journey, went through Divic. We reached Zvornik. In Zvornik we could only see two persons going down there toward the Drina, and they were using a pedestrian passageway towards Drina, and we continued our journey toward Karakaj. When we reached Karakaj, the lorries and buses turned left toward Tuzla. I was still hopeful that the exchange would take place, that we would be taken in between the lines, and that we would be listed, because we had not been listed up to that point. I was still hopeful as we were setting out toward Tuzla that we would be exchanged. We -- the drive was a short one, for maybe five or six minutes, and the vehicles turned right. At that point, it immediately dawned on me that we were not going in the direction of Tuzla but in the direction of Krizevici. Next, the vehicles pulled up. As soon as the vehicle was emptied, it went back. As we were getting close, we could see a school playground or a school yard there, and there were between 30 and 50 Serb soldiers there. And then we realised that this was indeed a UN APC, but it had been captured by the Serbs. It was parked in the yard to the left side. There were two soldiers in the UN blue uniforms and two Serb soldiers there, and there was a civilian who was aged above 50 and he was walking with them. They removed the UNPROFOR insignia, but they had the C in the insignia, which stands for S in Cyrillic, and this was the only thing that was visible on the APC plates. As we were -- as people were getting out of the vehicles, they had to run toward the school. I was wearing a leather jacket, and as I went out of the lorry I was told by a man there that I should take the jacket off and just throw it there on the ground, and I did. As I entered the building, the school building, we turned left along the corridor, which was about 10 metres. We had to run through the corridor, and then one reached a door leading to a large hall. People there were mostly from Potocari. They were elderly people; the average age was 70. I knew them. We were filling up the ranks, and so it went along. When the place was filled up, there were four young boys there and there was a grey blanket there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Let me ask you a few questions about what you've been telling us, and then you can continue to tell us what happened to you. You said earlier that while you were on this journey and you thought, hopefully, that you were heading towards Tuzla to be exchanged that you hadn't been listed yet and no one had been listed. What did you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110
utterances.text: I meant to say that no exchange could be carried out before people were listed because the Serbs didn't know how many people they had. Not a single one of us was registered by them. They can't even know our numbers. Only if they counted the dead bodies could they know how many people there were. They can't know how many people they killed, and it's true, they can't know, because nobody asked for our names. There was this one person, there were probably officers among them, who asked whether there was anyone from the Zvornik municipality amongst us. But nobody responded to that call and they asked no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Again, please slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. I think you answered my question. Then you said --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And if -- having gone through the transcript, I don't think there is an indication in it where we are, where is this building where they happened to --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: You're correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So if you could address that --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: That's where we're going. Could you tell us -- well, first of all, this area you've been describing, you've described the journey from Bratunac to Zvornik to Karakaj and then left and ended up at this place where you saw a school building. Which village were you in when the truck stopped and you saw the school?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110
utterances.text: This was Grbavci or Orahovac, whichever way you want it. I know that previously this place was called Grbavci; now it is called Orahovac. I don't know whether the area now called Orahovac is larger than it was previously, but I know that before this was called the Grbavci elementary school.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And if he could also confirm the date for us, please, now.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110
utterances.text: It was Friday, the 14th of July, I believe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Next question I want to ask you is about the soldiers that you said were in UN uniforms. Who were they? Were those UN soldiers?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110
utterances.text: No, they were Serb soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: How could you tell that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110
utterances.text: I know that because they didn't tell us anything, and they wore automatic rifles produced by Zastava, from Kragujevac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Incidentally, while we are at this, this is something that we discussed this morning and which I was meant to communicate to you at some point in time in anticipation of several mentions. We will be, in the course of this trial, have -- be referring to various kinds of weaponry and other military equipment. What I would like you to do as Prosecution is to compile a -- a document, a dossier, which would indicate a picture or a diagram of the various weapons and kinds of weaponry and tanks or armoured vehicles, whatever was in use in the former Yugoslavia at the time, and to which witnesses will be referring as we go along. Please, before you hand it over to the Trial Chamber, make it available to all the Defence teams so that we ascertain that they agree. I see Mr. McCloskey on his toes. Is there already such a document?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, as you know, you will soon see a video of many of these events, and we have a book of video stills that goes along with it that have the APCs, the weapons, but we will -- as you say, we will get a nice list for you.
