But for your knowledge, the -- the classic Zastava automatic weapon that is used is recognisable worldwide. You will -- it's an AK-47.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Right. But we have no military background in the least, and although of course from other cases I know what an APC is and I've heard about Zastava and so on and so forth, we will be coming across various descriptions. And in the past there have also been some disagreement between Prosecution and Defence on the correct nomenclature and description of some weapons. So if there is agreement on this, it will make everyone's life much easier. Yes, Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Of course when I hear the word "dossier" I get scared because it's not something I'm familiar with and I don't like very much. But if my colleague wants to produce a listing with pictures of weapons and types of weapons, I think that could indeed be useful, however, I wouldn't like that he would say who was using whatever weapon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: But to know it, to have a picture and a name of a weapon, I think that may be useful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I have a specimen myself which I can show you, let you have, and see whether you will agree to something similar to that, and you can bring it up-to-date or work on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We can bring weapons in the courtroom, if you would like.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, I don't think we need tanks and helicopters.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I mean handguns, but there's very clear video of all this. I think if we can leave weapons out of the courtroom, that would be nice. But we do have this weapon down in evidence if there is any need.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't think there is any need for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You have a weapon as well, Your Honour? It's nice to be aware of that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. So let's -- sorry for that interruption, Mr. Nicholls. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Were you able to observe how these soldiers with Zastavas were interacting with the Serb soldiers you saw there who were in Serb -- who were in normal army uniforms?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110
utterances.text: Let me tell you, there was no difference there because the Serb soldiers -- the other Serb soldiers also carried Zastava weapons, and they were good-quality weapons. Of course they only had side-arms - none of them had Howitzers or anything else - because they were confronted with people who were unarmed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Maybe I didn't ask the question well. Thank you. That helps to clarify, but were the UN -- were the soldiers dressed in UN uniforms behaving any differently than the other soldiers there or were they all acting kind of the same way?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110
utterances.text: They reacted in no way whatsoever, and there was a civilian there who was an interpreter, but there was no reaction on their part whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: How many soldiers total at the school did you see, speaking now about when you got off the truck?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110
utterances.text: Between 30 and 50 soldiers; quite a few of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. Now, I was going to get to it a little bit later, but I'll try to do it now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. If I may interrupt you, Mr. Nicholls. I'm curious about this interpreter reference. Answering your question, he said that these soldiers, which previously he said were Serbs dressed in UN uniforms, were not behaving or reacting in any way whatsoever. And then he mentions: "And there was a civilian there who was an interpreter." What's the significance of that? Because if we're talking of Serb soldiers wearing UN uniforms and Bosnian Muslim captives, what's the purpose of having an interpreter there?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: How did you know this person was an interpreter? Can you describe this civilian; what they were doing and who they were?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110
utterances.text: Let me tell you how I knew that. That's the way the UNPROFOR works. They always have a civilian who interprets for them, but these were people impersonating UN personnel, and that's why they had this person there who posed as an interpreter. But he was not an interpreter, in fact, he was a Serb just as all the other Serbs there, even those who were there to force us out of the truck. They parked the APC there, took the UNPROFOR insignia off. Instead of an UNPROFOR registration plate, there was just a plate with the letter C there, because Serbs using Cyrillic, C stands for S.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. So -- just so I'm clear, there was a civilian there, and your impression was that this person was there to look as though there was an interpreter?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110
utterances.text: It was just -- he was just there for pretense.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. I'd like to now show you four photos and see if you recognise the place in the photos. And we're going to try to do this on e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: If I could ask the court officer for 1691 is the first number.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Sir, this will - or should - appear on the screen in front of you. It's not there yet; it may be there in a minute.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I do have hard copies, Your Honour. Not for everybody, but in case we need them.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the school at Grbavci or Orahovac. This here is the sports hall. In this part here, the lorries were parked where people were taken off.

utterances.text: All right. Thank you very much.

utterances.text: All right. Will you be requiring him to make more markings on this?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't know if this is acceptable: I would suggest, maybe just for today, that we put -- that he write his witness number, PW-110, if that's okay, and we can figure something else out later.

utterances.text: All right. If you're happy with that. Are you happy with that? I see Mr. Haynes tempted to say something, but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Not really. Just in case there's another PW-110, perhaps he should put the indictment number on it as well, but no, I'm happy.

utterances.text: No problem, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Here?

utterances.text: [Interpretation] 110?

utterances.text: Dobro. Thank you. And we can mark this document as Prosecution Exhibit -- next number, 20 --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour. That will be Exhibit Number P2102, under seal -- I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Does it have to be under seal at this point in time?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. So it's P2102. Thank you. So we've solved that problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. All right. Good point. You haven't tendered, as yet, the clean picture, Mr. Jones -- not Mr. Jones, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Excuse me for the interruption, Your Honour. Perhaps it would save time if at the end of the witness's cross we could just offer the ones that we --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: -- think are appropriate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. For the record, however, we'd just like to point out that the witness made his marks on a photograph that carries ERN number 0046-1633. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: The next photo I would like to show you, sir, is number 1692. Sorry, before we do that -- before we do that. The photo I showed you that you've made markings on, it's still up there, not the one you marked. But is that a fair, accurate, representation of the Grbavci school as you remember it in July, 1995? Is there anything major that's different that you want to point out?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110
utterances.text: I don't know what the school building looked like from the outside. I know that I was there during the on-site investigation. The building was the same. A couple of old cabinets had been thrown away, and the area where the trucks were, the -- this part was walled up in the meantime. But all the rest was just the same as before.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. Everything was the same other than some cabinets missing and some kind of wall where the trucks were parked. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110
utterances.text: Yes. At the spot where we were taken out from the room, there was a lorry parked there. It was like with a ramp waiting for us to board it. When I returned four years later, I believe, this particular part where we came up from was walled up. All the rest was the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. And we'll talk about that ramp a little bit later.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Could I have 1692 now, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right, sir -- now don't touch the screen yet -- but again do you recognise the building here we've just been -- the building in front of you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110
utterances.text: Yes, I do. This is the sports hall and the auxiliary building that we all had to go through.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And is there anything on this photo which you would like to draw our attention to? Otherwise, you don't need to mark anything on it if you've already explained this well.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110
utterances.text: No. I just wanted to say that this was -- that this is a sports hall and the auxiliary room. This was all there. At the front was the place where we exited from that building. There is nothing special to say about this picture.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Meek.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Mr. President, I don't know if this is important, but before we took the last exhibit away from the witness - I'm looking at page 68, line 21 and 22 - the witness indicated, "This particular part where we came up from was walled up." And he didn't mark that -- 67, page 67, line 21, 22. That was never marked before the previous exhibit, 1691, was taken away from the witness. So perhaps he could mark it on this photograph, if it is in fact visible.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls. Thank you, Mr. Meek.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I didn't think that was necessary because he'd indicated where the trucks were parked, if I recall by the number 3, he said that was where the wall was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: -- so I thought the record was fairly clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think there are no walls here anyway, so let's proceed. For the record, however, the last photo that the witness has referred to was 0040-9640. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. We all agree that it is not necessary to go back to this photo and see where the wall is. Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Let me -- just to be -- let me ask one question about that wall then. Was it directly at the same place where the trucks were parked on the outside or was it somewhere else in relation to this school building? Was the wall where the trucks were parked or was it somewhere else?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110
utterances.text: No, no. As we were taken away blindfolded, in this corner the TAM lorry was parked. I know the lorry very well. This is where it was parked, and I don't know how they had done that. I believe that the podium is somewhat higher, as we climbed on the lorry we did not have to take a large step. A TAM lorry is some metre from the ground, so if we had to climb in from the ground, we would have had to take a long step. Since we didn't have to do that, I believe they had built something like a podium.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. So I think that was perhaps a translation, interpretation. There was a ramp there or a podium to help people get onto the truck, but not a wall. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110
utterances.text: I don't know whether in the meantime this thing has been destroyed in the meantime. This was walled up later on. This wall or podium had been built before we arrived, and then it was all walled up. In 1992, it was walled -- it was -- in 1998 it was walled up, but it was just the bricks. So I believe that that podium had existed before for us to climb on the vehicle.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Can we go back to 1691 just --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I think I do need to clear this up, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Let me ask you this: The ramp or podium, what was that made out of?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110
utterances.text: You know what? This was something as high as your desk. It was a structure. I believe this was not done at the moment when the building was built. This may have been done a day two before, and that's why they had destroyed that part of the wall. They just broke through one part of the wall, and this is where the lorry was parked to facilitate the climbing up. If you're blindfolded, how are you supposed to climb onto a lorry, if the lorry is high, if there is no construction to help you get onto the lorry?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Could we go now to the next photo, which is 1694. We have 1697.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Oh, you do have 1694, can we bring that up, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, because I think we have -- okay. Now it's changing.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And I'll say for the record, this photograph has the ERN number 00409650.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Sir, take your time, take a look at that photo. Do you recognise what is depicted in this photograph?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110
utterances.text: You can see the windows of the sports hall, and you can see something like a basket for basketball.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Is there any difference that jumps out to you of what you see in this photograph that you remember from the sports hall in July 14th, 1995?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110
utterances.text: Let me put it this way: I can describe the entrance into the sports hall. On the right-hand side there was a wall with the windows at the top. Then on the left-hand side there was an opening leading into the auxiliary room. This is the opening that we had to go through blindfolded. The easiest for me is to look at a photo, but when I look at this picture, I can only tell you that this is a sports hall with windows and the basket, which is either drawn onto the fall or fixed onto the wall. At the time when I was there, I don't remember this basket being there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now could we assign this an exhibit number and give it 169 -- and then go to the next photo, 1697. Actually, sorry, he didn't mark it, so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Are you going to mark this one now or are you going to stick to what you said earlier, that you will tender everything or whatever later on?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: We will tender it later. I'm sorry, Your Honour, I'd forgotten. If we could go to 1697.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, one moment because I recognise Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Now, the witness has indicated that this is a gym --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Sports hall, he said.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: -- and windows --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The word I heard in the translation was sports hall.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Or -- yes, sports hall, sorry, but he indicated that this is -- I'm not sure if he used it, I don't have the transcript here, he used sports hall, but he did not recognise this as being the sports hall he was in. If later on my colleague asks for this photo to be given an exhibit number, we would not object, but we would like the witness to know whether he recognises this - yes or no - as the place where he was held. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls, could you --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I think he explained his reaction to it, but I will ask again.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Do you recognise this photo? Can you tell from the photo whether it's the same sports hall you were held in on July 14th, 1995? And if you can't, just say you can't.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110
utterances.text: Yes, yes. This is where I was. I was in no other sports hall. That's where I was. They did not take me all over Zvornik to see some other sports hall. This was the sports hall where we were kept as cattle, sitting on the floor, on the wooden floor. I don't know what was on the floor. I did not dare look around -- what was around me. This is the sports hall where I was held.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Do you remember, if you do, where you sat in relation to these large windows we can see in the photo?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110
utterances.text: I was the closest to the auxiliary building, to the entrance into that auxiliary building that everybody had to go through. I was not sitting close to the big wall, but I was closer to the other, smaller wall.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Last one, then; 1697.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Again, Witness, take a look. Take your time and tell me if you recognise this place.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110
utterances.text: Yes, that's the sports hall in the school where we were kept.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: That's 00816804 [Realtime transcript read in error "00816801"] is the ERN number.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. Now, I briefly want to ask you some questions, Witness, about your experiences in the sports hall at the Grbavci school. You started off saying that you were forced to run into the school from the lorry.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: What happened when you went into the school? I think you said your jacket was taken from you. What was taken from you and what was the process as you entered the school?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110
utterances.text: They took the jacket, and previously, when I was captured, they took away the rucksack. And when I arrived at the school there was nothing left to take away from me. The only thing that they could -- that they could have taken away was my soul, but fortunately enough, they didn't do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Was anything taken from other prisoners as they entered the school?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110
utterances.text: The clothes. Some had to take their shirts off. They were probably not allowed to put their shirts back on. There was nobody like that in our lorry, but there was a very thin, elderly man who was shirtless. There were a number of shirtless men, but we were not forced -- the others were not forced to take their shirts off. They only told me to take my leather jacket off.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, Mr. Nicholls, and again apologies for interrupting you, but line 14 on the previous page, page 73. The ERN number of the document is wrong. It's not 00816801, but it is 00816804. That's just for the record. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, we've seen pictures of the room. How full was the sports hall when you entered it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110
utterances.text: When I entered, over half of it was full. And when everybody entered, there was very little space left. But we all sat down crunched and squeezed. We were sitting so tight that we could not move from the place that we were assigned.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: From the time that you entered the sports hall, how long did prisoners continue to arrive?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110
utterances.text: Five, six minutes, maybe even more. We were towards the back of the column, but all this happened very fast. As you jumped off the vehicle from either the lorry or the bus, before us there was a Centrotrans Sarajevo bus with the registration plates that I saw for the first time in the Cyrillic. We had never had Cyrillic registration plates before. It was then that I saw that Sarajevo registration with two C's, and also a Zvornik bus. At the time, they had special registration plates in Cyrillic, and it was only later on that we were all ordered to use the same Latinic registration plates.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And once all the prisoners, as far as you could tell, had arrived and had been -- and had run into the school, how many prisoners do you think were in the sports hall, approximately?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110
utterances.text: Anything between 500 and a thousand.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Where were the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can we be more precise? Because anything between 500 and 1.000, 1.000 is double of 500, so ...

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes. Just think about it for one moment and see if you can be more precise. If you can't, then that's fine.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110
utterances.text: Let me tell you this: If I had known what would happen and what -- that I would survive, I could count people. I could add up the width of every person times the number of heads, but just like with the Serbs, the Serbs didn't know exactly how many we were. They never made our list. They didn't know how many we were. We don't know how many we were. Maybe somebody was counting in secret. I can only draw my conclusion on the length of the convoy. If everybody from the convoy had been put there, then there must have been a thousand. But if people were separated, then they -- there were fewer of us. But a lot of elderly people who arrived before us filled up half of the room, and then the rest of us who had arrived on the lorries on that day, we filled the sports hall up. There were a lot of vehicles parked ahead of our vehicle, and a lot stopped after our vehicle. I don't know how many.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. You said there was some elderly people. Can you tell us the approximate age range of the prisoners in the room, from the youngest to the oldest, people that you saw.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110
utterances.text: The youngest was 15 and the oldest around 70. And that person, the oldest person, was from my village and he was aged 70 at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Let me ask you to think about that. How young was the youngest person in the room?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110
utterances.text: Save for the four children who were there, the four children that were there, one child was 10 and the oldest of the children was 14. But they were separated from us.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: How were they separated, these four children?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110
utterances.text: We were sitting in lines, and they were sitting next to the entrance door. And they faced the rest of us. The whole crowd was facing these four children who were sat by the main door.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, during this time you were there, these hours, were there guards at the door at the entrance?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110
utterances.text: Yes. Very young lads who were holding rifles in their hands. Somebody addressed them as soldiers, and they said they were not soldiers. They said that they were Karadzic's Chetniks, Young Chetniks. That's -- they took pride in that. When somebody addressed them as soldiers, this is what they said. Sometimes they would shoot in the air when there was commotion among the people, then they would shoot into the walls and into the ceilings. And we could still see the traces of those bullets when we went to the sports hall later on for field inspection.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour, are we stopping now or are we going another five minutes?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's up to you. If it's more convenient for you to break now, we can break now.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'll continue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We've got another five minutes to go.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This inspection that he's just referred to, field inspection, could he tell us when it occurred.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'll -- I was going to get to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: When you said this field inspection, you said "we," can you tell us now, after leaving the Grbavci school on the 14th of July, 1995, when did you go back to the school and who did you go with?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110
utterances.text: I apologise. I did not understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'm sorry. You said a field inspection. When you came back to the school you could still see traces of bullet holes from when the soldiers had fired into the walls of the school. When was that you went back to the school?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110
utterances.text: Oh, yes. This happened in 1999, sometime in the autumn of that year. I don't know the exact date. I believe that there is a record of that. There were two Campagnolas, the United Nations Campagnolas, and a big transporter and SFOR troops, and the person who took -- who made the record, and there was an interpreter as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, again, similar question I've asked you before: While you were in the school, was any food provided, was any medical care provided while you were a prisoner, and to the other prisoners?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110
utterances.text: No. Nobody offered us any food. Some prisoners were asked to bring water, but there were just too many of us. If they started from one end, they could only give water to two lines of people. So we were always thirsty. If you didn't experience that, then you can never know that water is the most beautiful thing in the world. Nobody wanted bread, but if somebody had brought you water, I believe that we would have drank 2 litres at once. That's how important water is, and that's why I'm saying today that water is more important than bread. We were thirsty, and if you've never been thirsty, you don't know the feeling. You cannot imagine the feeling.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: What was the temperature like in the school that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110
utterances.text: I don't know. It was the 14th of July, the hottest period of the year. It was very difficult to tell, but you know when you enter a room full of people, even if it had been cold outside, the room would have been heated up by the bodies of all of us in the room. And I believe that the outside temperature was well in its 30s.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And did any of the prisoners appear to you to need medical care?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110
utterances.text: Yes. People were complaining about feeling faint. I also wanted to have more water. I -- but if anybody was feeling faint or sick, the only thing that they would do was for that person to move a bit further where they could be given water, and that's all the assistance we ever got from them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. So my last question before we take a little break, sir: What kind of toilet facilities were provided for all the people in this room?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110
utterances.text: They gave us a bucket, but it was hot so nobody really felt the urge to relieve themselves. It was just too hot. There were maybe a few elderly people and a woman, maybe they used the bucket. The rest of us didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I think it's time for the break, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Nicholls. We'll have --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Excuse me, not "and a woman." It is not good translated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: It is line 10.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Elderly people and -- "elderly people and a woman."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: No, the women are mentioned in the -- in another context.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Witness, if you could -- I'll read it out to you. If there is a mistake -- if there is a mistake, please point it out to us. "They gave us a bucket, but it was so hot so nobody really felt the urge to relieve themselves. It was just too hot. There were maybe a few elderly people --" and then we have in the transcript "... and a woman. Maybe they used the bucket."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So what is the correct testimony?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I apologise to the women who are here in the room. I didn't say that there was a woman. I just apologised to the women in the room for mentioning that there were people who did relieve themselves in the bucket, because I mentioned that action. I wanted to apologise to the women in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, sir. We'll have a 20-minute break starting from now. Thank you. Same precaution as before. If the guard could kindly ask -- all right. The lady is leaving.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Sir, while you were in the sports hall, could you see whether there was any physical abuse of the prisoners? And ...

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110
utterances.text: No. Only one man was slapped about. Why, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: At any time while you were there, did any officers, senior officers, arrive at the school that you could see?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110
utterances.text: At the time I was there, some people arrived in civilian clothes. They stood on one side, observing us. When the time came for us to set out, a group of them gathered - I don't know whether they were civilians or soldiers - and one of them asked, as I said previously, whether there was anyone from the Zvornik municipality among us. Later on, I don't know whether it was this same person who put the question before someone else, when there was commotion in the hall, he said: Shut up, everyone. And we did. And then he said: Four rows in the hall stand up. These were mostly the elderly people I talked to you about. They stood up. He told them to take the right turn and face the wall, turning their back to the entrance. The next four rows had to do the same thing. This way they faced the exit they were supposed to take. As they approached my row, they issued the following order: Four rows stand up, and we were supposed to face the other wall, adjacent to the previous one. And in this way they lined us up. As you enter the hall, somewhere to the right in the middle of the hall, a person said: These people should not be killed. One of the Serb guards standing at the entrance replied by saying: Who says so? And then this same person repeated: These people should not be killed. This person wore only black trousers and, I believe, a shirt. Nothing else. The soldier retorted: Well, we'll see whether they should be killed or not. He said: Come along. He took the person, the man, out of the school building. We heard a rifle shot. The man started moaning. They took out another man, a younger man than the previous one. He was maybe 30 years old. He was also taken out, we could hear a rifle shot, and the man never returned. The persons carrying water were also prisoners, and they were at that point prohibited from going out to fetch water, probably because this was an attempt to conceal the crime. At a certain point later on a man wearing a red beret showed up --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Stop, stop, stop. It's running out of hand, Mr. Nicholls. Unless you control your own witness, we'll have to control him ourselves. The question was a very simple, straightforward one: At any time while you were there, did any officers, senior officers, arrive at the school that you could see? And instead of answering that question, he has given us an entire description of events that he was not asked to describe. So this is something that we cannot -- we cannot -- I'm not -- sir, one moment --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This other person was supposed to say that I should stand up, too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Be patient, be patient. We will get there when the time arrives. But in the meantime, please try to answer the questions that are put to you and not answer questions that are not put to you. Mr. Meek.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Again, I would just renew my objection I made earlier today, and if you would look at page 82, line 3 and 4, the witness again is speculating on why someone did something. It's pure speculation. He should leave that out, those extraneous comments like that. That's my objection, Your Honour. "Probably because this was an attempt to conceal the crime."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But he is an --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We don't agree with your objection, Mr. Meek. He is -- if that is the impression he formed at the time and he wants to relate it to us the way he considered it to be, he has every right to do so. However, what we definitely want rectified is the mode -- system we are proceeding with. At least we will try to interrupt as least -- the least we can, but at the same time try to control your own witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And just a brief statement, and it's -- when we -- when this witness first testified many years ago, it was under a different system. The -- the Judge preferred not to hear much from the lawyers, and they were pretty much just allowed to tell their story, and that's, I think, partly what this witness is doing. We got closer to the question and answer the last time, and so I think he understands this, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: -- that's part of the problem here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, I appreciate that, Mr. McCloskey, and that is -- provides a reasonable answer. But at the same time, the truth of the matter is that he has not answered the question. Of course, what he has been telling us is important, and we will need to come to it, but he also needs to answer the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I understand that, Your Honour, and I can certainly break it up more. I was letting the witness go a little bit longer because I thought it was easier for him to explain things that way and I was going to come back, but I will try to break this up a little bit more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: So, Witness, please try to have a little bit shorter answers, and we'll go through this step by step, what happened to you. I understand you are trying to tell us what you think is important that happened to you that day. Now, I had asked you about whether any officers appeared, and I believe - it's off my screen - but you said: No, but some people dressed in civilian clothes came and started giving orders to the prisoners. Is that right, that you didn't see any senior officers?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110
utterances.text: No. No. It wasn't people in civilian clothes who arrived. Actually, the civilian people came into the room before the military men were to come. Of course there were officers coming in, because after they came in, the process of taking people out started. Because from the auxiliary building a bag of rags was brought in, rags that were used to blindfold us. And of course there must have been a command issued, because otherwise they would not have proceeded to do that. It was after their arrival that the people were being taken out.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: When the officers came, did you see them inside the sports hall or were they looking in? Can you just describe how you could tell these officers had arrived.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110
utterances.text: It was after they issued an order to that effect, because it was them who lined the people up, and they lined it up so that they faced in the other direction. They had their backs turned to the door and their face to the other end of the hall. When the soldiers went away, probably the people who were left behind there had received orders from them to take the people out.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Let me just be clear, and I think this will be the last question on this topic: It was the officers who made the orders [Realtime transcript read in error "officers"] for the people to line up and which way they should face. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110
utterances.text: Whether they were officers, probably yes. I didn't observe their ranks, but they regulated the whole matter, and once they went away, the process of taking people out started.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And were --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. Is he capable of distinguishing between an officer and a soldier?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: That's what I was going to ask.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: If they were wearing --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah, one moment. Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Just because the -- what is on the transcript at line 6, page 85, line 6, "It was the officers who made the officers for the people to line up." I heard something like it was the officers who gave the orders, but I'm not sure that this is not clear. "The officers who made the officers for the people to line up." Could you clarify this, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Bourgon. Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yeah, I believe I said it was the officers who made the orders for the people to line up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think so, too, but I think Mr. Bourgon is also right, so let's proceed. I think it's clear enough, but let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Could you see the uniforms of the -- these men who you said you thought were giving these orders and -- I'll just ask that for now.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110
utterances.text: You see, in wartime, all people wore camouflage uniforms and one could not distinguish between ordinary soldiers and officers, save for the fact that the officers had ranks. I wasn't able to observe the ranks. I know that previously the uniforms worn by officers were different from those of ordinary soldiers, whereas in this particular period they all wore equal camouflage uniforms. I know that their officers wore rank insignia on top of their shoulders, and I know that these others had some sort of insignia on their jacket pockets.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I think that clears it, Your Honour, that he --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, no, he's your witness, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, you started talking about this, about some blindfolds earlier. I want you to describe how you and the other prisoners left the gym. What happened? What was the process of leaving? And now I'm just talking about how you leave the gym and go outside of the gym or sports hall.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110
utterances.text: When the order came, they brought a bag of rags or strips of cloth that were maybe some 50 centimetres wide -- some 5 centimetres wide -- or rather, 15 centimetres wide. And they asked prisoners to put these blindfolds on each other. Near to the entrance there were two armed soldiers wearing camouflage uniforms and there was one woman wearing a camouflage uniform. And the woman gave every prisoner a glass of water after they had put a blindfold on. Why, I don't know. Anyway, they had guards, two guards, placed at the entrance so that they may control the flow of people. It all went along very quickly.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: A little bit slower, please. Continue.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110
utterances.text: The person who escorted people to be executed wore a red beret, he was quite young, and he didn't speak to anyone. He would go away with the lorry. I don't know whether he was in the cabin of the lorry or under the tarpaulin. I only know that he escorted people to be executed. When my turn came, at this point we were told that all of us had to pass through. And this was sometime in the evening that I stood up. I was blindfolded. I was given water by the woman. I boarded a lorry, and it was -- I was on the right-hand side close to the cabin, the driver's cabin. There was a bench -- or actually, there were two benches running along the two sides, and the lorry was full of people. I don't know whether there were 30, 40, or 20 of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Just one moment, please. Thank you. That's very clear. I wanted to ask you a couple of questions. You talked earlier about a ramp or something that was used by the prisoners to get on the lorry. Can you describe how high --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... this TAM truck was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110
utterances.text: I can't tell you how long the ramp was or how high it was, but it may have been a metre above the ground, although we did not have the impression of climbing high. I did -- of course didn't have occasion to measure the height, but it was -- the ramp lay more or less at the height of the TAM truck.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Now, of course the witness now has just mentioned the word "TAM truck," but the first time that this was ever mentioned was by counsel, and I think in this way we are leading the witnesses in terms of describing. He always referred to that truck as being a lorry and he never said the word "TAM truck," Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I recall having on my transcript "TAM truck" much earlier on in the day.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: That's my recollection, too, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, definitely. But I can assure you, Mr. Bourgon, that it has been mentioned earlier on. Yes, Mr. Krgovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if I may be of assistance, the witness mentioned the term "TAMic," small TAM, but it was at a different point in time and in a different context.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's continue. Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: One moment. Just for your record, Your Honour, page 69, line 17, the witness talks about being taken away blindfolded, and in the corner there was a TAM lorry, T-A-M, and it was parked, and then he starts talking about the podium.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Nicholls. Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. Please describe now how many men were sitting in the back of the TAM lorry and where they sat once you had been placed on your blindfold.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110
utterances.text: I told you that there were two benches. I can't tell you how many people can be seated on these benches. While people were boarding, we still had our blindfolds on, and then as people -- other people got on, there was no space on the benches. They occupied the floor between the benches. People asked where these people were being taken, and the answer was to the camp at Bijeljina, and after that no further questions were asked.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Just to be clear here, who asked where the people were being taken? Was that the prisoners or somebody else?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110
utterances.text: Yes, yes. The prisoners themselves. As soon as they started boarding these people, the question was put as to where the people were being taken, and the answer was to the Bijeljina camp. After that, nobody asked any more questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Are you familiar with TAM trucks from before the war or before you were placed on this one? Had you seen one before?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110
utterances.text: TAM lorries were small lorries normally owned by farmers to transport agricultural products, and TAMic is what we use to refer to a 2-ton lorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, the one you were on, how many men do you think would fit in the back with you at the time you were there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110
utterances.text: At least 30 people; ten on each of the benches and ten of them on the floor between the benches. I think 30 of them can fit.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. How far did the truck travel once you'd been -- once you had gotten into the back with these other men?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110
utterances.text: The trip was quite short. I didn't know where we were being taken to at the time. We had our blindfolds on. In my estimate, the lorry headed to the left and it drove for a while along the gravel road. We shook quite hard at the beginning, and then at a certain point it pulled up. We could hear the voices of people outside. We were then ordered to get off the bus. We did. We were then lined up. I don't know whether we were lined up in one or two rows. Shooting started. I could hear a burst of fire from the right-hand side, and I was positioned at the left. And the shots came from the right-hand side. People started falling over, and I fell down with them and I had my arm over the chest of the man next to me. Then there was one person saying: We should finish them off. And the other person saying: Take it easy, take it easy. Then shots were fired again upon people lying down. I have a scar here, which was probably just a piece of gravel that hit me, and then the shooting stopped. Then I could hear shouts to the effect that: We should start taking their watches off, and so on and so forth. Then others saying: No, we are not going to do that. At any rate, I didn't have a watch on me at that time. Then there was another lorry that arrived. The shooting was heard again, and some 10 to 15 minutes later there was another truck arriving. It was getting dark at that point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Stop here for the time being. I didn't want -- Mr. Lazarevic, that's why I asked you to wait, because I didn't want to interrupt the witness at such a crucial moment. But perhaps you could now tell us --

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I notice something in the transcript that I haven't heard from the witness, actually, it is rather different, and it deals with this moment when certain person asked the soldier to finish him off. Here it says that -- well, allegedly one of the soldiers said: Finish them off. What I heard was the person was begging. If Mr. Nicholls could clarify this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls, you've been able to follow. Perhaps you can put a direct question on this.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Let me go back over a little bit of what you said, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It does make a difference, obviously, because one would be a Serb, the other one would not be a Serb.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Line 20, 21.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Perhaps I can assist Mr. Nicholls. It's on page 90, line 20, 21.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I've got it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: You said, sir, after the shooting had taken place and you'd fallen down, that there was one person saying, and this is what the transcript says: We should finish them off. And another -- and the other person was saying: Take it easy, take it easy. Can you tell me what you heard when you were lying on the ground at that time.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110
utterances.text: No. There was one person who had been hit that said: Finish me off. And then the other person saying: Take it easy, take it easy. So it wasn't the persons who were shooting at people who said that; it was rather the person who was shot that said that, and then the other person telling him: Take it easy, take it easy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So that clarifies the matter. I thank you, Mr. Lazarevic, for pointing it out. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And again, I mean, our attention is being drawn that he is going too fast. He needs to slow down a little bit further.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I'm told that was a translation error.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, you said you heard somebody saying: Take it easy, take it easy. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Who was that? Is that a --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110
utterances.text: It was the Serb soldier who was performing the killing.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Just so this is clear, he was saying that in response to the person saying: Finish me off? Are these statements connected?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, you said that you were slightly injured and you pointed at a part of your body. Could you show the Court where you were injured and, just to make it clear, tell us what that injury was.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110
utterances.text: Yes. Right here between the fingers.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. So for the record, he pointed to his right hand, just between the first and second finger.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And that wasn't a severe injury from what -- if I gather you correctly?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110
utterances.text: Most probably a stone was set in motion by a burst of fire and got me on my hand, and I was lucky that it was just that slight wound.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, you described hearing trucks coming, gun-fire, trucks leaving every ten minutes or so. How long did that continue for, you could hear these -- these trucks moving and then gun-fire?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110
utterances.text: Let me tell you, this was in the early evening and went on until it was completely dark. I don't know whether it took two hours or thereabouts. The people gathered next to the excavator that was excavating a pit there, (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Stop.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'd ask for a redaction, actually, Your Honour, of lines 20 through 22. I think it will be clear why I'm asking for that a little bit later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's redact lines 21 and 22, please, thank you. After -- actually, we can start from after the words "excavating a pit there," and you redact the rest from those two lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And that will need us -- require us to have a 30-minute break when you finish, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: When -- now, you've described laying there for a few hours and hearing these things. At any point did you take your blindfold off or were you still blindfolded while you were hearing these shots and trucks coming and going?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110
utterances.text: When it got really dark and when they went to a different meadow, I took the blindfold off. The man who was lying over me, I didn't mind that so much while it was still day-time. When it got dark and his body got really cold and rigid, I couldn't feel my legs, they went numb(redacted)

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Stop.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: If we could just take that name out, Your Honour, and I will take care of this part --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the President, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Sorry about that. Lines 16 and 17, we redact everything that goes after the words "they went numb."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Can we perhaps go into private session?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think it will be safer to do that because I can see where you're going, so it will be easier for him because he can't distinguish --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- really between one question and what he's anticipated to answer in the next one. So let's go into --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are in open session, Mr. Nicholls, and please make sure that the witness understands you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And I'll say it again, Witness: Please don't mention the names of the people that we just finished talking about or their nicknames while we were in private session. All right. Tell me what happened next after you said these -- there was a discussion which you had overheard. What happened next? What did you do?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110
utterances.text: They left to this other meadow. The three men stayed behind. Later on some -- at a distance from me to there was some 300 metres. I could hear shooting. In the meantime, a lorry came under light, and it shone its lights on us, and all of them who had been killed were clearly visible, and it parked next to the person excavating the pit and they started talking amongst each other, and I couldn't hear them because both machines' engines were on. And when that person with the lorry arrived --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour, could we go back into private session for one minute?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's go back to private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, we are back in open session. Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'm sorry I interrupted you, sir. You were telling us that some of the men left, and then a lorry came and shone its lights on the area.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110
utterances.text: It was not a lorry. It was a loader truck.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. A loader came. Please continue telling the Court what happened when the loader truck came.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110
utterances.text: When this lorry came, there was a person alive next to the excavator. He jumped on his feet, started running towards the woods. Shots were fired after him. The person who came with the loader truck turned his lights on the area of the forest where that person had fled into. I moved at that moment and I heard the words to the effect of: There is another person running away. Luckily enough, nobody heard him and maybe he thought that he had just imagined, as his lights were shining across the bodies. I looked around. Nobody was walking towards me. I moved just twice, and I started crawling. I turned around to see if anybody was following me, and then I jumped on my feet. I saw a stone --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you for stopping. The transcript said: "Luckily enough, nobody heard him." I'm not sure, is that right? Did you mean nobody heard you, or did you mean nobody heard somebody else?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110
utterances.text: Those who were standing guard, the Serb soldiers who had been killing, did not hear him say that there was somebody else alive.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. I understand. And just one follow-up question. The transcript said "loader truck" and I used that word "loader truck." Can you describe what a loader is, what it looks like.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110
utterances.text: It's a construction machine that loads material onto lorries. It has a hoe the capacity of which is 2 cubic metres. It's a very good machine that is used in construction. It's not used for anything else but for loading construction material onto -- onto trucks. And this is a very good machine for loading trucks.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, if you could please continue. Tell us in your own words how you escaped from this field, from where you were.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110
utterances.text: And then when I stood up, I started running along the stone -- I didn't know where I was. I didn't know what was there. And when I climbed onto that stone, there was a rail track. I crossed the rail track. I fell down the bank. Luckily enough, I ended up in a cornfield. I ran through -- halfway into the cornfield. And then I realised that the corn was moving, and I was afraid that they would see me. Then I started crawling and I hid in a little thicket. I could hear the water, but I couldn't see any water. The Serb soldiers who were standing guard ran around the cornfield. They fired shots but probably in the air. I could hear the bullets and I could hear the bullets breaking branches. But then they returned. I was there all that time. And when all the shots stopped, I -- I was thinking I know where I had been taken to, but when I was blindfolded, I no longer knew where I was taken, whether towards Zvornik or where. And when everything was quiet, I stood up, I started walking, and I was most afraid when I left the cornfield that I would be awaited there by somebody. Luckily enough, there was nobody there. I climbed onto the railroad. I didn't know whether to go down the railroad or up the railroad. I decided to go down the railroad. And then I arrived in the same place. I arrived at a railway station. The door was open, leading to a room. There was nothing there, nobody there. I saw a village there which I didn't recognise, and I knew I was not supposed to go there. I returned the same way: I went down to the road by a well that was in the other meadow, and I saw the other group of people that had been killed. That was the other meadow where the soldiers had gone previously to kill the rest of the people.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. We've got to finish in a few minutes. Witness, if I understand, you left and ended up back at the same place, at the same area and saw another field with dead bodies in it. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110
utterances.text: That is right, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: How far apart were these two fields?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110
utterances.text: Some 300 metres, not more.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Difficult to say maybe, but how many bodies did you see in this field?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110
utterances.text: Let me tell you, the bodies were prostrated across the meadow. Most of the area was covered. I don't know how many bodies were there. There was a man who was barely alive who was separated away from the rest of the bodies. And the sounds he produced were not human sounds. They were more like animal sounds. And he was the only person who was a bit away from the rest of the group. The people -- the bodies that were there prostrated on that ground were either on their backs or on their bellies, but they were spread out. That's how they had fallen when they were shot.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And you said there was a well or something like that by the road by this field. Did I understand you right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110
utterances.text: Yes. It was a source of water, ever-running water that people used to water their cattle. It was like a well that was taking care of the people.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have very little more, but I think maybe if I could just finish that up in the first ten minutes tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I think that will be better.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: It's virtually finished.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That will be better because this has been a long session. So I think the witness can be escorted out of the courtroom. Sir, you will return tomorrow. We haven't finished as yet. There will be a few minutes more when Mr. Nicholls, hopefully, will conclude his examination-in-chief; and after that, we will start with the various cross-examinations. I'll explain to you tomorrow. In the meantime, you will be attended to. Important thing is that you're not to communicate with anyone on the matters that you are testifying upon.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls and various Defence teams. I mean, I've made a rough calculation. Two hours and a half has -- have already become three hours and 35 minutes. So I'm not pushing you, of course, because this is just the beginning and one understands that we will need to be as flexible as possible, but at the same time try to conclude, because obviously then we will need to ask the various Defence teams whether they stand by their time schedule for cross-examination or whether they would like it revised. So we will deal with all this tomorrow morning at 9.00. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
